title: Live captions for town council meetings
Caption timing in fast dialogue scenes
Speaker labels in group captions
Reading speeds for children's captions
Extended audio description for lectures
Describing on-screen text in news broadcasts
Audio description scripts written by volunteers
Synthetic voices for audio description
Sound cues as visual indicators in shooters
Subtitles for game cutscenes and menus
Haptic alerts for doorbells and alarms
Plain-language summaries of court rulings
snippet: Our town council asked for live captions in its public meetings. We share what it took…
Fast dialogue breaks caption timing rules. We tested three timing strategies with deaf viewers…
Group conversations need speaker labels. We compared names, colors and positions…
Children read captions more slowly than adults. We measured reading speeds by age…
Lectures leave little room for description. Extended description pauses the video…
News broadcasts put text on screen that blind viewers miss. We described it in the gaps…
Volunteers wrote audio description scripts for a regional theater. Here is how we trained them…
Synthetic voices can read description scripts. We compared them with human narrators…
Shooters signal danger with sound. We turned the key sounds into visual indicators…
Cutscenes and menus often lack subtitles. We audited thirty games…
Doorbells and alarms can buzz a phone or a wristband. We tested patterns deaf households prefer…
Court rulings are hard to read. We wrote plain-language summaries and tested them…

drafts.title: One script for captions and audio description
drafts.text: Caption files and audio description scripts are written by different people from the same picture, and they drift apart: a sound the captions name is a sound the description talks over. We merged them into one timed script with three kinds of line, for speech, for sound and for picture, and let each output take the lines it needs. This talk shows the format, the review workflow and what changed for viewers who use both.
drafts.notes:
Helps: deafblind viewers and anyone using captions and description together
Barrier: two scripts that contradict each other
Standard: WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.2.2 and 1.2.5

drafts.title: Doorbell haptics for game sound cues
drafts.text: Games show sound cues as icons at the edge of the screen. We tried the vibration patterns deaf households already know from doorbell and alarm alerts instead, so a player feels footsteps behind them as the pattern for the front door.
